claim: Sperm competition occurs commonly across many invertebrate and vertebrate taxa.
source: Sperm competition (Parker, 1970) occurs commonly across many invertebrate and vertebrate taxa and is a potent evolutionary force influencing male reproductive biology (Birkhead and Møller, 1998; Birkhead and Pizzari, 2002; Simmons and Fitzpatrick, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature on sperm competition across taxa.

claim: Sperm competition is a potent evolutionary force influencing male reproductive biology.
source: Sperm competition (Parker, 1970) occurs commonly across many invertebrate and vertebrate taxa and is a potent evolutionary force influencing male reproductive biology (Birkhead and Møller, 1998; Birkhead and Pizzari, 2002; Simmons and Fitzpatrick, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on the evolutionary significance of sperm competition.

claim: Sperm competition theory predicts that males will trade-off between energy expended making high-quality ejaculates with obtaining mating opportunities.
source: Sperm competition theory predicts that males will trade-off between energy expended making high-quality ejaculates with obtaining mating opportunities and that males will invest differentially in ejaculates with respect to sperm competition risk (Parker, 1990; Parker et al., 1997; Parker, 1998; Wedell et al., 2002; Birkhead et al., 2009; Parker and Pizzari, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on sperm competition.

claim: Males will invest differentially in ejaculates with respect to sperm competition risk.
source: Sperm competition theory predicts that males will trade-off between energy expended making high-quality ejaculates with obtaining mating opportunities and that males will invest differentially in ejaculates with respect to sperm competition risk (Parker, 1990; Parker et al., 1997; Parker, 1998; Wedell et al., 2002; Birkhead et al., 2009; Parker and Pizzari, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on sperm competition.

claim: Males of many species can make rapid adjustments to ejaculate quality within days.
source: In agreement with these predictions, males of many species can make rapid adjustments to ejaculate quality within days (Rudolfsen et al., 2006; Pizzari et al., 2007; Thomas and Simmons, 2007; Gasparini et al., 2009; Smith and Ryan, 2011), hours (Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007a) and even minutes (Kilgallon and Simmons, 2005; Joseph et al., 2015) of exposure to a new social cue that signals changing sperm competition risk, such as the presence of a female, or a male competitor.
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies demonstrating rapid ejaculate adjustments.

claim: Males of many species can make rapid adjustments to ejaculate quality within hours.
source: In agreement with these predictions, males of many species can make rapid adjustments to ejaculate quality within days (Rudolfsen et al., 2006; Pizzari et al., 2007; Thomas and Simmons, 2007; Gasparini et al., 2009; Smith and Ryan, 2011), hours (Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007a) and even minutes (Kilgallon and Simmons, 2005; Joseph et al., 2015) of exposure to a new social cue that signals changing sperm competition risk, such as the presence of a female, or a male competitor.
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study demonstrating rapid ejaculate adjustments.

claim: Males of many species can make rapid adjustments to ejaculate quality within minutes.
source: In agreement with these predictions, males of many species can make rapid adjustments to ejaculate quality within days (Rudolfsen et al., 2006; Pizzari et al., 2007; Thomas and Simmons, 2007; Gasparini et al., 2009; Smith and Ryan, 2011), hours (Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007a) and even minutes (Kilgallon and Simmons, 2005; Joseph et al., 2015) of exposure to a new social cue that signals changing sperm competition risk, such as the presence of a female, or a male competitor.
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies demonstrating rapid ejaculate adjustments.

claim: In fowl, males of dominant social status strategically allocate sperm, ejaculating more and faster swimming sperm in initial copulations and to females of higher quality.
source: For example, in fowl (Gallus gallus), males of dominant social status strategically allocate sperm, ejaculating more and faster swimming sperm in initial copulations and to females of higher quality (Pizzari et al., 2003; Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2006; Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007a; Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007b), and alter their allocation strategy accordingly when changing social status (Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on fowl sperm allocation.

claim: Fowl males alter their sperm allocation strategy when changing social status.
source: For example, in fowl (Gallus gallus), males of dominant social status strategically allocate sperm, ejaculating more and faster swimming sperm in initial copulations and to females of higher quality (Pizzari et al., 2003; Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2006; Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007a; Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007b), and alter their allocation strategy accordingly when changing social status (Cornwallis and Birkhead, 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on fowl sperm allocation.

claim: Males of several vertebrate species ranging from fish to humans can strategically alter the quality of their ejaculate in response to social cues.
source: While males of several vertebrate species ranging from fish (Rudolfsen et al., 2006; Gasparini et al., 2009; Smith and Ryan, 2011) to humans (Kilgallon and Simmons, 2005; Joseph et al., 2015) can strategically alter the quality of their ejaculate in response to social cues, the mechanism behind such rapid adjustments is as yet unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies across vertebrate taxa.

claim: The mechanism behind rapid ejaculate adjustments in response to social cues is unknown.
source: While males of several vertebrate species ranging from fish (Rudolfsen et al., 2006; Gasparini et al., 2009; Smith and Ryan, 2011) to humans (Kilgallon and Simmons, 2005; Joseph et al., 2015) can strategically alter the quality of their ejaculate in response to social cues, the mechanism behind such rapid adjustments is as yet unknown.
evidence: Explicitly stated as unknown in the manuscript.

claim: A promising candidate mechanism for rapid adjustment of sperm velocity may be found in the non-sperm component of the ejaculate, particularly if such adjustments occur more rapidly than spermatogenesis.
source: A promising candidate mechanism for rapid adjustment of sperm velocity may be found in the non-sperm component (seminal fluid and its constituents) of the ejaculate, particularly if such adjustments occur more rapidly than spermatogenesis (Cameron et al., 2007; Perry et al., 2013; Fitzpatrick and Lüpold, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on seminal fluid and spermatogenesis timing.

claim: Seminal fluid is a complex medium containing a great diversity of molecules.
source: Seminal fluid is a complex medium containing a great diversity of molecules (Poiani, 2006; Juyena and Stelletta, 2012) and is known to influence sperm velocity and motility in vertebrates (Lahnsteiner et al., 1998; Lahnsteiner et al., 1996; Poiani, 2006; Locatello et al., 2013; González-Cadavid et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on seminal fluid composition.

claim: Seminal fluid is known to influence sperm velocity and motility in vertebrates.
source: Seminal fluid is a complex medium containing a great diversity of molecules (Poiani, 2006; Juyena and Stelletta, 2012) and is known to influence sperm velocity and motility in vertebrates (Lahnsteiner et al., 1998; Lahnsteiner et al., 1996; Poiani, 2006; Locatello et al., 2013; González-Cadavid et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on seminal fluid effects.

claim: In grass goby, large males that adopt a guarding strategy have a greater concentration of the seminal fluid glycoprotein mucin.
source: For example, research using an externally fertilising fish, the grass goby (Zosterisessor ophiocephalus), compared males for which sperm competition strategy is determined by age/size and found large males that adopt a guarding strategy have a greater concentration of the seminal fluid glycoprotein mucin (Scaggiante et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on grass goby.

claim: In grass goby, seminal fluid from sneak males decreases the velocity of rival guard male sperm.
source: Furthermore, by separating and recombining seminal fluid and sperm from different males, research using the same species found seminal fluid had a tactic-specific effect on sperm velocity, with seminal fluid from sneak males decreasing the velocity of rival guard male sperm and seminal fluid from guard males increasing the velocity of sneak male sperm (Locatello et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on grass goby.

claim: In grass goby, seminal fluid from guard males increases the velocity of sneak male sperm.
source: Furthermore, by separating and recombining seminal fluid and sperm from different males, research using the same species found seminal fluid had a tactic-specific effect on sperm velocity, with seminal fluid from sneak males decreasing the velocity of rival guard male sperm and seminal fluid from guard males increasing the velocity of sneak male sperm (Locatello et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on grass goby.

claim: In fowl, ejaculates produced by males allocated to females of higher quality contained faster sperm.
source: However, only one study to date has investigated the role that seminal fluid plays as a mediator of short-term plastic sperm performance in a vertebrate species using fowl and the results were inconsistent with theoretical expectation: Cornwallis and O'Connor, 2009 found that while ejaculates produced by male fowl that were allocated to females of higher quality contained faster sperm, seminal fluid from those ejaculates reduced the velocity of sperm from the same male allocated to females of lower quality.
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on fowl.

claim: In fowl, seminal fluid from ejaculates allocated to higher quality females reduced the velocity of sperm from ejaculates allocated to lower quality females.
source: However, only one study to date has investigated the role that seminal fluid plays as a mediator of short-term plastic sperm performance in a vertebrate species using fowl and the results were inconsistent with theoretical expectation: Cornwallis and O'Connor, 2009 found that while ejaculates produced by male fowl that were allocated to females of higher quality contained faster sperm, seminal fluid from those ejaculates reduced the velocity of sperm from the same male allocated to females of lower quality.
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on fowl.

claim: Evidence that seminal fluid mediates the rapid plastic adjustment of an ejaculate's motile performance consistent with theoretical expectation is lacking.
source: Thus, although there is evidence that seminal fluid can influence sperm velocity, evidence that seminal fluid mediates the rapid plastic adjustment of an ejaculate's motile performance consistent with theoretical expectation is lacking.
evidence: Explicitly stated as lacking in the manuscript.

claim: In salmonids, fertilisation occurs externally.
source: In salmonids, fertilisation occurs externally and sperm competition occurs in the majority of spawnings (Berejikian et al., 2010; Sørum et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of salmonid reproductive biology.

claim: In salmonids, sperm competition occurs in the majority of spawnings.
source: In salmonids, fertilisation occurs externally and sperm competition occurs in the majority of spawnings (Berejikian et al., 2010; Sørum et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on salmonid spawning.

claim: Male chinook salmon adopt Alternative Reproductive Tactics situationally, as 'hooknose' males fight to establish social dominance.
source: Male chinook salmon adopt Alternative Reproductive Tactics (ARTs) situationally, as 'hooknose' males fight to establish social dominance (Esteve, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on chinook salmon reproductive behavior.

claim: Only dominant male chinook salmon guard spawning females thus obtaining priority in mating position.
source: Only dominant males guard spawning females thus obtaining priority in mating position, while subdominant males that lose contests attempt to sneak fertilisations by invading spawning pairs and releasing their sperm (Esteve, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on chinook salmon reproductive behavior.

claim: Subdominant male chinook salmon that lose contests attempt to sneak fertilisations by invading spawning pairs and releasing their sperm.
source: Only dominant males guard spawning females thus obtaining priority in mating position, while subdominant males that lose contests attempt to sneak fertilisations by invading spawning pairs and releasing their sperm (Esteve, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on chinook salmon reproductive behavior.

claim: The social status of male salmon is subject to change over the course of a spawning season.
source: The social status of male salmon is subject to change over the course of a spawning season; for example, in coho salmon (O. kisutch), 22% of observed contests between hooknose males resulted in displacement of the previous dominant male (Healey and Prince, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on coho salmon.

claim: In coho salmon, 22% of observed contests between hooknose males resulted in displacement of the previous dominant male.
source: The social status of male salmon is subject to change over the course of a spawning season; for example, in coho salmon (O. kisutch), 22% of observed contests between hooknose males resulted in displacement of the previous dominant male (Healey and Prince, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on coho salmon.

claim: When males engage in sperm competition, sperm swimming speed is the primary predictor of fertilisation success in chinook salmon.
source: Previous research has shown that when males engage in sperm competition, sperm swimming speed is the primary predictor of fertilisation success in chinook salmon (Evans et al., 2013; Rosengrave et al., 2016) and other salmonids (Gage et al., 2004; Liljedal et al., 2008; Egeland et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on chinook salmon fertilisation success.

claim: Sperm swimming speed is the primary predictor of fertilisation success in salmonids.
source: Previous research has shown that when males engage in sperm competition, sperm swimming speed is the primary predictor of fertilisation success in chinook salmon (Evans et al., 2013; Rosengrave et al., 2016) and other salmonids (Gage et al., 2004; Liljedal et al., 2008; Egeland et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on salmonid fertilisation success.

claim: Sperm competition theory predicts subdominant males, which have greater sperm competition risk, will invest in ejaculates with faster swimming sperm than dominant males.
source: Sperm competition theory therefore predicts subdominant males, which have greater sperm competition risk, will invest in ejaculates with faster swimming sperm than dominant males and males changing social status should adjust their investment accordingly (Parker, 1990; Parker et al., 1997; Parker, 1998; Wedell et al., 2002; Birkhead et al., 2009; Parker and Pizzari, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on sperm competition.

claim: Males changing social status should adjust their ejaculate investment accordingly.
source: Sperm competition theory therefore predicts subdominant males, which have greater sperm competition risk, will invest in ejaculates with faster swimming sperm than dominant males and males changing social status should adjust their investment accordingly (Parker, 1990; Parker et al., 1997; Parker, 1998; Wedell et al., 2002; Birkhead et al., 2009; Parker and Pizzari, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on sperm competition.

claim: In Arctic charr, subdominant males produce ejaculates with more sperm and faster swimming sperm than dominant males.
source: Indeed, several studies that experimentally manipulated social status using Arctic charr (Salvelinus alpinus) have found that subdominant males produce ejaculates with more sperm and faster swimming sperm than dominant males (Liljedal and Folstad, 2003; Rudolfsen et al., 2006; Vaz Serrano et al., 2006; Haugland et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on Arctic charr.

claim: Following a social challenge in Arctic charr, sperm concentration and velocity decreased over a 4-day period compared with pre-trial levels in dominant males.
source: Furthermore, Rudolfsen et al. (2006) demonstrated that following a social challenge, both sperm concentration and velocity decreased over a 4-day period compared with pre-trial levels in dominant males, and observed an increase in sperm concentration but no change in sperm velocity for subdominant males.
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on Arctic charr.

claim: Following a social challenge in Arctic charr, sperm concentration increased but sperm velocity did not change for subdominant males.
source: Furthermore, Rudolfsen et al. (2006) demonstrated that following a social challenge, both sperm concentration and velocity decreased over a 4-day period compared with pre-trial levels in dominant males, and observed an increase in sperm concentration but no change in sperm velocity for subdominant males.
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on Arctic charr.

claim: Ejaculates from subdominant Arctic charr sire the same number of eggs when in competition with ejaculates from dominant males if their sperm were released after the average delay observed under natural conditions.
source: Recent research shows that ejaculates from subdominant Arctic charr sire the same number of eggs when in competition with ejaculates from dominant males if their sperm were released after the average delay observed under natural conditions (Egeland et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on Arctic charr.

claim: Salmonid males in disfavoured mating positions can compensate by producing more competitive ejaculates than dominant males.
source: These results suggest that salmonid males in disfavoured mating positions can compensate by producing more competitive ejaculates than dominant males, but whether males changing social status adjust their sperm velocity, and if such adjustments to ejaculates are mediated by sperm or non-sperm components of the ejaculate, is yet to be determined.
evidence: Inferred from cited research on Arctic charr and supported by citation.

claim: Whether males changing social status adjust their sperm velocity is yet to be determined.
source: These results suggest that salmonid males in disfavoured mating positions can compensate by producing more competitive ejaculates than dominant males, but whether males changing social status adjust their sperm velocity, and if such adjustments to ejaculates are mediated by sperm or non-sperm components of the ejaculate, is yet to be determined.
evidence: Explicitly stated as undetermined in the manuscript.

claim: Whether adjustments to ejaculates are mediated by sperm or non-sperm components of the ejaculate is yet to be determined.
source: These results suggest that salmonid males in disfavoured mating positions can compensate by producing more competitive ejaculates than dominant males, but whether males changing social status adjust their sperm velocity, and if such adjustments to ejaculates are mediated by sperm or non-sperm components of the ejaculate, is yet to be determined.
evidence: Explicitly stated as undetermined in the manuscript.

claim: Subdominant males had on average faster swimming sperm than dominant males.
source: Subdominant (S) males had on average faster swimming sperm (Average Path Velocity, or VAP) than dominant (D) males.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The difference in sperm velocity between subdominant and dominant males was not significant when social status was initially determined in stage 1.
source: This difference was not significant when social status was initially determined in stage 1 (Table 1; Figure 2a) but was significant for stage 2 (Table 1; Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 1 and Figure 2a.

claim: The difference in sperm velocity between subdominant and dominant males was significant for stage 2.
source: This difference was not significant when social status was initially determined in stage 1 (Table 1; Figure 2a) but was significant for stage 2 (Table 1; Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 1 and Figure 2b.

claim: There was considerable variation in sperm swimming speeds among males.
source: Overall, there was considerable variation in sperm swimming speeds among males, accounted for by the random predictor 'male identity' that was significant in both stages (stage 1: χ2(1)=105.11, p<0.001; stage 2: χ2(1)=70.02, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Sperm concentration was significantly higher in subdominant males than in dominant males in stage 1.
source: Additionally, sperm concentration was significantly higher in S than in D males in stage 1 (Table 1; Figure 3a), but not stage 2 (Table 1; Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3a.

claim: Sperm concentration was not significantly different between subdominant and dominant males in stage 2.
source: Additionally, sperm concentration was significantly higher in S than in D males in stage 1 (Table 1; Figure 3a), but not stage 2 (Table 1; Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 1 and Figure 3b.

claim: Sperm concentration for males that remained subdominant (SS) was significantly higher than for those males that remained socially dominant (DD) in stage 2.
source: However, sperm concentration for males that remained subdominant (SS) was significantly higher than for those males that remained socially dominant (DD) in stage 2 (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 1.

claim: There was a significant increase in mean VAP for males that changed from dominant to subdominant social status (DS).
source: There was a significant increase in mean VAP for males that changed from dominant to subdominant social status (DS; Table 2; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 2 and Figure 4.

claim: There were no other significant changes in either VAP or sperm concentration for males of the other social phenotypes.
source: Throughout the social status experiment, there were no other significant changes in either VAP or sperm concentration for males of the other social phenotypes (Table 2; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 2 and Figure 4.

claim: There was a significant overall interaction effect between social phenotype and experimental stage on VAP.
source: There was also a significant overall interaction effect between social phenotype and experimental stage on VAP (χ2(3)=11.8, p=0.008), with a significant interaction effect found only for males changing from dominant to subdominant status (DS; p=0.02, 95% CI = 2.9–34.9).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A significant interaction effect was found only for males changing from dominant to subdominant status (DS).
source: There was also a significant overall interaction effect between social phenotype and experimental stage on VAP (χ2(3)=11.8, p=0.008), with a significant interaction effect found only for males changing from dominant to subdominant status (DS; p=0.02, 95% CI = 2.9–34.9).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no significant interaction effects between social phenotype and experimental stage on sperm concentration.
source: We found no significant interaction effects between social phenotype and experimental stage on sperm concentration (χ2(3)=3.0, p=0.385).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The social status of the rival male was a significant predictor of the difference in VAP between focal male's sperm incubated in their own seminal fluid and the focal male's sperm incubated in their rival's seminal fluid.
source: Within each dyad, the social status of the rival male was a significant predictor of the difference in VAP between focal male's sperm incubated in their own seminal fluid and the focal male's sperm incubated in their rival's seminal fluid (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 3.

claim: Seminal fluid from subdominant males increased the sperm swimming speed of sperm from dominant males.
source: Seminal fluid from subdominant males increased the sperm swimming speed of sperm from dominant males, conversely, the seminal fluid from dominant males decreased sperm swimming speed of the sperm from subdominant males (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Seminal fluid from dominant males decreased sperm swimming speed of the sperm from subdominant males.
source: Seminal fluid from subdominant males increased the sperm swimming speed of sperm from dominant males, conversely, the seminal fluid from dominant males decreased sperm swimming speed of the sperm from subdominant males (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Incubating sperm in the seminal fluid of a rival with faster VAP increases that male's sperm velocity.
source: However, rival's social status was no longer significant (Table 3) when the difference in VAP between the focal male control and rival male control was added as a fixed predictor to the model, for which a significant positive linear relationship was detected (Table 3), with sperm in the seminal fluid of a rival that had faster VAP increasing sperm velocity and sperm in the seminal fluid of a rival that had slower VAP decreasing sperm velocity relative to VAP in their own seminal fluid (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 3 and Figure 6.

claim: Incubating sperm in the seminal fluid of a rival with slower VAP decreases that male's sperm velocity.
source: However, rival's social status was no longer significant (Table 3) when the difference in VAP between the focal male control and rival male control was added as a fixed predictor to the model, for which a significant positive linear relationship was detected (Table 3), with sperm in the seminal fluid of a rival that had faster VAP increasing sperm velocity and sperm in the seminal fluid of a rival that had slower VAP decreasing sperm velocity relative to VAP in their own seminal fluid (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 3 and Figure 6.

claim: Male social status was a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired.
source: Male social status was a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired (Table 4), with subdominant males siring a greater proportion (0.54 ± 0.08 95% CI, n = 21) than dominant males (0.46 ± 0.06 95% CI, n = 21).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 4.

claim: Subdominant males sired a greater proportion of eggs than dominant males.
source: Male social status was a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired (Table 4), with subdominant males siring a greater proportion (0.54 ± 0.08 95% CI, n = 21) than dominant males (0.46 ± 0.06 95% CI, n = 21).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 4.

claim: The social status of the seminal fluid donor when seminal fluid was swapped between males was a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired.
source: The social status of the seminal fluid donor when seminal fluid was swapped between males was also a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired (Table 4), with sperm incubated in the seminal fluid of subdominant males siring a greater proportion (0.6 ± 0.09 95% CI, n = 21) of eggs than sperm incubated in the seminal fluid of dominant males (0.4 ± 0.09 95% CI, n = 21).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 4.

claim: Sperm incubated in the seminal fluid of subdominant males sired a greater proportion of eggs than sperm incubated in the seminal fluid of dominant males.
source: The social status of the seminal fluid donor when seminal fluid was swapped between males was also a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired (Table 4), with sperm incubated in the seminal fluid of subdominant males siring a greater proportion (0.6 ± 0.09 95% CI, n = 21) of eggs than sperm incubated in the seminal fluid of dominant males (0.4 ± 0.09 95% CI, n = 21).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 4.

claim: The difference in sperm velocity between competitors was a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired in both unmanipulated and recombined ejaculate seminal fluid treatments.
source: The difference in sperm velocity between competitors was also a significant predictor of the proportion of eggs sired in both unmanipulated (Table 4) and recombined ejaculate seminal fluid treatments (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 4.

claim: The change in relative sperm velocity between males within the same male-male-female combinations across seminal fluid treatments was a significant predictor of the change in the proportion of eggs sired by that male's sperm across treatments.
source: The change in relative sperm velocity between males within the same male-male-female combinations across seminal fluid treatments was a significant predictor of the change in the proportion of eggs sired by that male's sperm across treatments (Table 4; Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Table 4 and Figure 7.

claim: Males with the highest risk of sperm competition produced ejaculates with both higher sperm concentration and faster swimming sperm.
source: In this study, we experimentally manipulated social status to produce four social phenotypes with differing levels of sperm competition risk, and in accordance with sperm competition theory (Parker, 1990; Parker et al., 1997; Parker, 1998; Wedell et al., 2002; Birkhead et al., 2009; Parker and Pizzari, 2010), found males with the highest risk of sperm competition produced ejaculates with both higher sperm concentration and faster swimming sperm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and consistent with cited theory.

claim: Males can make rapid adjustments to sperm velocity in a strategic response to changes in social position that signal increased sperm competition risk.
source: We also found males can make rapid adjustments to sperm velocity in a strategic response to changes in social position that signal increased sperm competition risk.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Seminal fluid acts as a mediator of rapid strategic adjustment to sperm velocity.
source: While seminal fluid is often implicated to harbour the unknown mechanism behind plastic sperm performance in vertebrates (Perry et al., 2013; Fitzpatrick and Lüpold, 2014), our combined results for the first time, unequivocally demonstrate that seminal fluid acts as a mediator of rapid strategic adjustment to sperm velocity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from combined results.

claim: Strategic adjustments of sperm velocity mediated by seminal fluid directly impact male fitness.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate strategic adjustments of sperm velocity mediated by seminal fluid directly impact male fitness, highlighting the adaptive significance of plastic ejaculate performance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on fertilisation success.

claim: Males forced to change from dominant to subdominant social status responded by increasing sperm velocity within 48 hr.
source: We show males forced to change from dominant to subdominant social status, and therefore exposed to increased sperm competition risk, responded by increasing the quality of their ejaculate, in this case sperm velocity, within 48 hr (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Males forced to change from subdominant to dominant social status did not show a significant change in sperm velocity.
source: While we predict that males forced to change from subdominant to dominant social status, therefore exposed to decreased sperm competition risk, would respond by decreasing their ejaculate quality, we did not see a significant change in sperm velocity for these males.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Subdominant males that later became dominant had a relatively low mean sperm velocity that was more similar to dominant males than those from the other subdominant phenotype in the first stage of the experiment.
source: However, subdominant males that later became dominant had a relatively low mean sperm velocity that was more similar to dominant males than those from the other subdominant phenotype in the first stage of the experiment (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Subdominant males produced ejaculates with greater sperm concentration than dominant males.
source: Accordingly, we found subdominant males produced ejaculates with greater sperm concentration than dominant males.
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: There was no significant increase in sperm concentration for any of the social phenotypes over a 48-hr period.
source: However, our results show that there was no significant increase in sperm concentration for any of the social phenotypes over a 48-hr period.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The exact time taken for spermatogenesis in salmonids is unknown.
source: The exact time taken for spermatogenesis in salmonids is unknown; however, the process almost certainly takes more than 48 hr (Billard, 1983a; Billard, 1983b; Schulz et al., 2010).
evidence: Explicitly stated as unknown, with citations supporting the time estimate.

claim: Spermatogenesis in salmonids almost certainly takes more than 48 hr.
source: The exact time taken for spermatogenesis in salmonids is unknown; however, the process almost certainly takes more than 48 hr (Billard, 1983a; Billard, 1983b; Schulz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on spermatogenesis.

claim: The observed changes in sperm velocity are mediated by a component of the ejaculate that modifies the competitiveness of existing sperm, rather than simply via the production of new sperm.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that the observed changes in sperm velocity are mediated by a component of the ejaculate that modifies the competitiveness of existing sperm, rather than simply via the production of new sperm.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of changes relative to spermatogenesis duration.

claim: The observed plasticity of sperm velocity in chinook salmon is mediated by seminal fluid.
source: Our results clearly demonstrate the observed plasticity of sperm velocity in chinook salmon, a key determinant of fertilisation success in several vertebrate species (Birkhead et al., 1999; Malo et al., 2005; Gasparini et al., 2010; Boschetto et al., 2011) including salmonids (Gage et al., 2004; Liljedal et al., 2008; Evans et al., 2013; Egeland et al., 2015; Rosengrave et al., 2016), is mediated by seminal fluid.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from combined results.

claim: Sperm from the same male, when incubated in seminal fluid from different males, had significantly different sperm velocities.
source: We found sperm from the same male, when incubated in seminal fluid from different males, had significantly different sperm velocities, and the direction of this effect could be predicted by social status.
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: The direction of the seminal fluid effect on sperm velocity could be predicted by social status.
source: We found sperm from the same male, when incubated in seminal fluid from different males, had significantly different sperm velocities, and the direction of this effect could be predicted by social status.
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: When sperm from dominant males were incubated in seminal fluid from subdominant males, their sperm velocity increased compared to the baseline measures in their own seminal fluid.
source: For example, when sperm from dominant males were incubated in seminal fluid from subdominant males we found that on average their sperm velocity increased compared to the baseline measures in their own seminal fluid, and found the opposite effect when sperm from subdominant males were incubated in seminal fluid from dominant males (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: When sperm from subdominant males were incubated in seminal fluid from dominant males, their sperm velocity decreased compared to the baseline measures in their own seminal fluid.
source: For example, when sperm from dominant males were incubated in seminal fluid from subdominant males we found that on average their sperm velocity increased compared to the baseline measures in their own seminal fluid, and found the opposite effect when sperm from subdominant males were incubated in seminal fluid from dominant males (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The findings are consistent with the prediction that seminal fluid from ejaculates with faster swimming sperm will enhance the speed of sperm from ejaculates with slower sperm.
source: Contrary to Cornwallis and O'Connor, 2009, for which seminal fluid from higher quality ejaculates decreased the velocity of sperm from lower quality ejaculates in fowl, our findings are consistent with the prediction that seminal fluid from ejaculates with faster swimming sperm will enhance the speed of sperm from ejaculates with slower sperm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to theoretical prediction.

claim: The disparity between the findings in chinook salmon and those in fowl possibly reflect differences in the reproductive biology of these species.
source: The disparity between our findings and those in fowl (Cornwallis and O'Connor, 2009) possibly reflect differences in the reproductive biology of these species; including internal and external modes of fertilisation and differences in the structure and formation of social hierarchies and associated sperm competition risk.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about differences between species.

claim: Fertilisation occurs rapidly in salmonids, with the majority of eggs fertilised within 10 s post ejaculation.
source: Fertilisation occurs rapidly in salmonids, with the majority of eggs fertilised within 10 s post ejaculation (Hoysak and Liley, 2001; Liley et al., 2002; Yeates et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on salmonid fertilisation.

claim: Rapid fertilisation time frames in salmonids may allow for little interaction between seminal fluid and sperm from different males during spawning.
source: Such rapid time frames may allow for little interaction between seminal fluid and sperm from different males during spawning.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid fertilisation time frame.

claim: Research using Arctic charr found the activation of sperm with a solution containing seminal fluid from another male had no effect on sperm velocity.
source: This is supported by research using Arctic charr that found the activation of sperm with a solution containing seminal fluid from another male had no effect on sperm velocity (Rudolfsen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on Arctic charr.

claim: In chinook salmon, seminal fluid from precocious males significantly decreases the velocity of hooknose male sperm.
source: However, a recent experiment that separated and recombined ejaculates from precocious chinook salmon males (obligate sneakers) and adult hooknose males report similar results to those found in the grass goby, with seminal fluid from precocious males significantly decreasing the velocity of hooknose male sperm (Lewis and Pitcher, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on chinook salmon.

claim: Chinook salmon seminal fluid has not evolved a targeted effect on sperm from males adopting a different tactic within the same age/size class.
source: Our results suggest chinook salmon seminal fluid has not evolved a targeted effect on sperm from males adopting a different tactic within the same age/size class, as regardless of social status, males that have faster recorded sperm velocities produced seminal fluid that increases the velocity of sperm from other males with slower speeds, and likewise males with slower sperm velocity produced seminal fluid that decreases the velocity of sperm from males with faster speeds (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Males that have faster recorded sperm velocities produced seminal fluid that increases the velocity of sperm from other males with slower speeds.
source: Our results suggest chinook salmon seminal fluid has not evolved a targeted effect on sperm from males adopting a different tactic within the same age/size class, as regardless of social status, males that have faster recorded sperm velocities produced seminal fluid that increases the velocity of sperm from other males with slower speeds, and likewise males with slower sperm velocity produced seminal fluid that decreases the velocity of sperm from males with faster speeds (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Males with slower sperm velocity produced seminal fluid that decreases the velocity of sperm from males with faster speeds.
source: Our results suggest chinook salmon seminal fluid has not evolved a targeted effect on sperm from males adopting a different tactic within the same age/size class, as regardless of social status, males that have faster recorded sperm velocities produced seminal fluid that increases the velocity of sperm from other males with slower speeds, and likewise males with slower sperm velocity produced seminal fluid that decreases the velocity of sperm from males with faster speeds (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The influence seminal fluid has on sperm velocity translates to having an effect on male fitness.
source: In addition to demonstrating that seminal fluid influences sperm competitiveness, our in vitro sperm competition trials show the influence seminal fluid has on sperm velocity translates to having an effect on male fitness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on fertilisation success.

claim: Changes in the relative sperm velocity between competitors were significantly correlated with the change in the proportion of eggs sired by each male.
source: We measured the fertilisation success within the same male x male x female combinations across trials, and compared those males across unmanipulated and recombined ejaculate treatments, finding changes in the relative sperm velocity between competitors were significantly correlated with the change in the proportion of eggs sired by each male (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The change in sperm velocity due to the seminal fluid in which sperm were incubated had a significant influence on the proportion of eggs sired by those sperm.
source: That is, the change in sperm velocity due to the seminal fluid in which sperm were incubated had a significant influence on the proportion of eggs sired by those sperm, in some cases completely reversing the 'winner' of sperm competition within the same male-female group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on fertilisation success.

claim: In some cases, seminal fluid effects completely reversed the 'winner' of sperm competition within the same male-female group.
source: That is, the change in sperm velocity due to the seminal fluid in which sperm were incubated had a significant influence on the proportion of eggs sired by those sperm, in some cases completely reversing the 'winner' of sperm competition within the same male-female group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on fertilisation success.

claim: Natural variation in several seminal fluid metrics was not correlated with sperm velocity in chinook salmon, including pH, osmolality and ion composition.
source: Previous studies have found that natural variation in several seminal fluid metrics was not correlated with sperm velocity in chinook salmon, including pH, osmolality and ion composition (Rosengrave et al., 2009a; Flannery et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on chinook salmon.

claim: Seminal fluid may contain different levels of available nutrients therefore fuelling differential energy production in sperm.
source: It is possible that seminal fluid contains different levels of available nutrients therefore fuelling differential energy production in sperm.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: In the short term following activation of motility in salmonids, sperm utilise ATP as the energy source for flagellar movement.
source: In the short term following activation of motility in salmonids, sperm utilise ATP as the energy source for flagellar movement (Christen et al., 1987) using both stored ATP reserves and increasing ATP production significantly via aerobic respiration (Lahnsteiner et al., 1993, Lahnsteiner et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on sperm energy metabolism.

claim: Sperm ATP levels have been positively correlated with sperm velocity in external fertilisers.
source: Sperm ATP levels have been positively correlated with sperm velocity (Lahnsteiner et al., 1998; Bencic et al., 1999; Burness et al., 2004) and fertilisation success (Zilli et al., 2004; Vladić et al., 2010) in external fertilisers.
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on external fertilisers.

claim: Sperm ATP levels have been positively correlated with fertilisation success in external fertilisers.
source: Sperm ATP levels have been positively correlated with sperm velocity (Lahnsteiner et al., 1998; Bencic et al., 1999; Burness et al., 2004) and fertilisation success (Zilli et al., 2004; Vladić et al., 2010) in external fertilisers.
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on external fertilisers.

claim: Exposure to different levels of exogenous nutrients in seminal fluid while sperm are immotile in the testis may influence energy metabolism, influencing sperm velocity post activation.
source: Exposure to different levels of exogenous nutrients in seminal fluid while sperm are immotile in the testis may influence energy metabolism, for example altering available energy reserves or stored nutrient reserves, influencing sperm velocity post activation (Lahnsteiner et al., 1999).
evidence: Speculative reasoning with citation support.

claim: Seminal fluid may contain peptide or RNA signalling molecules that alter sperm behaviour.
source: Alternatively, seminal fluid may contain peptide or RNA signalling molecules, that alter sperm behaviour.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Chemotaxis in several marine invertebrates is controlled by signalling pathways that are initiated by chemoattractant peptides released by ova.
source: For example, chemotaxis in several marine invertebrates is controlled by signalling pathways that are initiated by chemoattractant peptides released by ova (Kaupp et al., 2003; Darszon et al., 2008; Evans and Sherman, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on marine invertebrate chemotaxis.

claim: Evidence is accruing that proteins and RNAs in seminal fluid exosomes may play critical roles in regulating sperm development and fertilisation.
source: Evidence is also accruing that proteins and RNAs in seminal fluid exosomes may play critical roles in regulating sperm development and fertilisation (Vojtech et al., 2014; Jodar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature on seminal fluid exosomes.

claim: Several Seminal Fluid Proteins have been associated with sperm velocity in vertebrate species.
source: Several Seminal Fluid Proteins (SFPs) have been associated with sperm velocity in vertebrate species (Lahnsteiner et al., 1996, 1998; Poiani, 2006) and are therefore likely candidates for modifying rapid adjustment of sperm velocity (Simmons and Fitzpatrick, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on seminal fluid proteins.

claim: Differences in SFP composition have been documented among males adopting different reproductive tactics in externally fertilising fish.
source: Differences in SFP composition have been documented among males adopting different reproductive tactics in externally fertilising fish (Scaggiante et al., 1999; Gombar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on fish SFPs.

claim: Males can tailor SFP composition in response to sperm competition risk.
source: Additionally, a growing body of empirical work has demonstrated that males can tailor SFP composition in response to sperm competition risk (Wigby et al., 2009; Fedorka et al., 2011; Ramm et al., 2015; Simmons and Lovegrove, 2017) and the mating status of females (Sirot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on SFP plasticity.

claim: Males can tailor SFP composition in response to the mating status of females.
source: Additionally, a growing body of empirical work has demonstrated that males can tailor SFP composition in response to sperm competition risk (Wigby et al., 2009; Fedorka et al., 2011; Ramm et al., 2015; Simmons and Lovegrove, 2017) and the mating status of females (Sirot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on SFP plasticity.

claim: The role of SFPs in sperm competition is generally poorly understood.
source: The role of SFPs in sperm competition, with the exception for some insect species (den Boer et al., 2010; Avila et al., 2011) and specific proteins in mammals (Ramm et al., 2008), is generally poorly understood.
evidence: Explicitly stated with citations to exceptions.

claim: The activity of SFPs associated with energy metabolism and respiration have been correlated with sperm velocity in a Cyprinid species.
source: While the activity of SFPs associated with energy metabolism and respiration have been correlated with sperm velocity in a Cyprinid species (Lahnsteiner et al., 1996) and rainbow trout (O. mykiss) (Lahnsteiner et al., 1998), total protein concentration as well as the activity of lactate dehydrogenase, anti-trypsin and superoxide dismutase enzymes were not correlated with sperm velocity in chinook salmon (Flannery et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies on fish SFPs.

claim: Total protein concentration as well as the activity of lactate dehydrogenase, anti-trypsin and superoxide dismutase enzymes were not correlated with sperm velocity in chinook salmon.
source: While the activity of SFPs associated with energy metabolism and respiration have been correlated with sperm velocity in a Cyprinid species (Lahnsteiner et al., 1996) and rainbow trout (O. mykiss) (Lahnsteiner et al., 1998), total protein concentration as well as the activity of lactate dehydrogenase, anti-trypsin and superoxide dismutase enzymes were not correlated with sperm velocity in chinook salmon (Flannery et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study on chinook salmon.

claim: The SFPs tested in chinook salmon represent only a small fraction of the enzymatic activity likely to occur in fish seminal fluid.
source: However, these SFPs represents only a small fraction of the enzymatic activity likely to occur in fish seminal fluid (Gombar et al., 2017; Nynca et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on fish seminal fluid composition.

claim: Male chinook salmon can make rapid adjustment to sperm velocity in response to social cues that signal changing sperm competition risk.
source: In conclusion, as predicted by sperm competition theory (Parker, 1990; Parker et al., 1997; Parker, 1998; Wedell et al., 2002; Birkhead et al., 2009; Parker and Pizzari, 2010), we find male chinook salmon can make rapid adjustment to sperm velocity in response to social cues that signal changing sperm competition risk and such changes have a significant impact on the outcome of sperm competition and therefore male fitness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and consistent with cited theory.

claim: Changes in sperm velocity have a significant impact on the outcome of sperm competition and therefore male fitness.
source: In conclusion, as predicted by sperm competition theory (Parker, 1990; Parker et al., 1997; Parker, 1998; Wedell et al., 2002; Birkhead et al., 2009; Parker and Pizzari, 2010), we find male chinook salmon can make rapid adjustment to sperm velocity in response to social cues that signal changing sperm competition risk and such changes have a significant impact on the outcome of sperm competition and therefore male fitness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on fertilisation success.

claim: Seminal fluid plays a key role in mediating the strategic rapid adjustment of sperm velocity even in a species with external fertilisation.
source: We further demonstrate that seminal fluid, even in a species with external fertilisation, plays a key role in mediating the strategic rapid adjustment of sperm velocity and for the first time provide strong evidence the mechanism behind plasticity in sperm velocity lies within the non-sperm component of the ejaculate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from combined results.

claim: The mechanism behind plasticity in sperm velocity lies within the non-sperm component of the ejaculate.
source: We further demonstrate that seminal fluid, even in a species with external fertilisation, plays a key role in mediating the strategic rapid adjustment of sperm velocity and for the first time provide strong evidence the mechanism behind plasticity in sperm velocity lies within the non-sperm component of the ejaculate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from combined results.

claim: Plastic adjustment of ejaculate quality in response to changing sperm competition risk is an effective evolutionary strategy in systems with dynamic social environments.
source: Our results support plastic adjustment of ejaculate quality in response to changing sperm competition risk is an effective evolutionary strategy in systems with dynamic social environments and we show seminal fluid mediates such adjustments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from results.

claim: Seminal fluid mediates plastic adjustments of ejaculate quality in response to changing sperm competition risk.
source: Our results support plastic adjustment of ejaculate quality in response to changing sperm competition risk is an effective evolutionary strategy in systems with dynamic social environments and we show seminal fluid mediates such adjustments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: A total of 17 sexually mature 3-year-old females and 44 sexually mature 3-year-old 'hooknose' males were studied.
source: We studied a total of 17 sexually mature 3-year-old females and 44 sexually mature 3-year-old 'hooknose' males captured between 27 April and 30 May in 2013, 2014 and 2015.
evidence: Explicitly stated sample sizes in the methods.

claim: A total of 11 social status manipulation trials were conducted each using four males.
source: A total of 11 social status manipulation trials were conducted each using four males (n = 44; Figure 1).
evidence: Explicitly stated experimental design in the methods.

claim: Male dominance was determined by calculating a Dominance Index using the number of aggressive interactions between males.
source: Male dominance was then determined by calculating a Dominance Index (DI; Winberg et al., 1991; Bailey et al., 2000; see Behavioural observations) using the number of aggressive interactions between males.
evidence: Explicitly stated methodology with citations.

claim: In 10 out of 11 pairs the status of males determined on the first day did not change from on the second day.
source: We found that in 10 out of 11 pairs the status of males determined on the first day did not change from on the second day.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 5.

claim: Average path velocity (VAP) was used as the measure of sperm swimming speed.
source: We used average path velocity (VAP, µm s−1) as our measure of sperm swimming speed which estimates the average velocity of a sperm cell for 0.5 s over a smoothed path (Rosengrave et al., 2008, 2009a, 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Explicitly stated methodology with citations.

claim: A total of 21 replicated in vitro fertilisation trials were conducted.
source: In 2014 and 2015, at both stages of the social status manipulation trials (Figure 1) we conducted a total of 21 replicated in vitro fertilisation trials to determine the effects of ejaculate recombination (seminal fluid) on male fertilisation success.
evidence: Explicitly stated experimental design in the methods.

claim: The fertilisation trials involved 24 individual males and 17 females.
source: This involved 24 individual males and 17 females in which sperm from the dominant and subdominant male in each dyad competed to fertilise a female's eggs.
evidence: Explicitly stated sample sizes in the methods.

claim: Approximately the same number of sperm per male (10^7 spermatozoa) were used in each fertilisation trial.
source: Sperm density was adjusted prior to each fertilisation trial so that approximately the same number of sperm per male (107 spermatozoa) were used in each trial.
evidence: Explicitly stated methodology in the methods.

claim: Three microsatellite loci (Ots 100, Ots 101, Oki 3a) were amplified in a multiplex PCR and used to determine paternity.
source: Three microsatellite loci (Ots 100, Ots 101, Oki 3a; Table 6) were then amplified in a multiplex PCR and used to determine paternity by manually matching alleles between offspring, mother and either potential sire.
evidence: Explicitly stated methodology in the methods.
